title: Jarvis
whatItDoes: Your memory, folders, photos, lists, calendar and Record in one place. Every request, typed or spoken, becomes a block: exactly what you said, a numbered ledger of every step it took, and what each step actually returned, rendered as the thing it is — a table, a page, a screenshot, a command's real output. Nothing is flattened into "Done" and nothing scrolls away; a block from an hour ago is still there and still re-runnable. Voice is always on rather than a button you press: it waits for its name, hears the sentence after it, and can be talked over mid-answer — with an echo test so it never replies to itself. The part no web assistant has: a local agent on the PC, so it drives a real Chromium that keeps your logins, runs shell commands, reads and writes files, lists and focuses windows, and sees the screen. It reads freely and stops for a yes on the one class of step that cannot be undone. With the agent off it still thinks, remembers and answers, and says plainly which capability is missing.
features: Photos look: "Cards, people first" (Nov 25 2026, picked from three coded mockups) — the Photos tab uses the Folders card look: an "All › Photos" header with "N photos · N people · N to review"; the agent instruction is one line (its example chips show while you type in it); the iPhone import panel and the "teach who's who" card became quiet chips ("Get photos from your iPhone" opens the full Import now / Autopilot panel; "N of N people recognisable", or an amber "Teach who's who" chip with no people yet, or one naming people without reference photos). The review queue sits under a Needs you heading. A People row shows each person's face (Profiles faces via `cachedFaces`, else their refs) and how many filed photos they are in (by `identityIds`, else name). Album cards show the newest three pictures as a cover, who is in them and when they last changed; the hover Edit button is unchanged.

Folders look: "Richer cards" (Nov 25 2026, picked from three coded mockups) — the folder home says what is inside each folder: counts by kind for everything nested under it (notes, files, logins, links, to-dos, websites), up to four sub-folder chips you can jump into, and "Updated … · <newest item>" (or "N items not backed up" in amber when a Google account is connected and some aren't on Drive). A summary line reads "N items · N folders · N levels deep". On screens 1024 px+ the folder tree is a docked left panel with indent guides (toggle remembered as `recall:tree-docked`); on a phone it stays the drawer. The Drive backup card became a quiet status chip in the toolbar (dot + "backed up 2 h ago") that opens the full card. An Ask Jarvis bar under the toolbar (⌘J) sends what is typed straight to the Folders agent and replaces the floating launcher while folders are on screen. Pure numbers in `src/lib/recall/folderStats.ts` (+ tests).

Folders is a RAG agent on the shared Jarvis harness (Nov 2026) — Ask Jarvis in Folders uses the same model pick as every Jarvis chat (`nj.chat-model:v1`, live across chats on the page via `jarvis:chat-model`), with a model menu in its header. *Claude · my subscription* goes to the PC agent's `/brain/claude` (raw mode, its own JSON); any other pick goes to `/api/recall` with that model. Retrieval (`src/lib/recall/rag.ts`): stemmed keyword hits, every item inside a folder the question names (any nesting depth), and an OUTLINE of every saved item (title, full path, gist, people in a photo) so the model finds things by meaning and asks to `read` up to 6 more items in a second pass. Answers name the folder path and list clickable Sources. "Organise this", "put this in Trading > Gold Strategies" and "find where this belongs" produce a Save to Folders card: exact destination step by step (missing folders marked NEW), why, the full text, a picker to send it elsewhere — nothing is written until Save here. A failed model call now says why (out of credit, timeout, bad model) instead of "AI is off"; that notice is only for a server with no key. The main chat has `folders_ask` (read-only Folders RAG) and `dashboard_add_note` takes nested paths, keeps the note's text (it used to save empty: it read `content`, the tool sends `body`), and always asks first on Ask/Trusted/Auto. Profiles' cloud brain follows the same model pick.

Backups: several Google accounts, real storage (Nov 2026) — the Drive backup card opens Accounts & storage: every connected Google account with its email, storage from Drive's own `about.storageQuota` (used / total / free, Drive vs Gmail & Photos vs Trash), the backup target, last successful backup, last run counts, and tabs for every backed-up file (its real Drive path, account, updated), Folders items not on any account, and failed/skipped items. Tokens stay in memory per account; the registry (`drive-backup-accounts:v1`) syncs without them. A backup made with the old single sign-in is adopted as an account automatically. When the PC agent is up, the panel also lists rclone remotes with their real storage (`POST /rclone/remotes`, read-only).

Camera Autopilot recognises people from Profiles (Nov 2026) — the people Autopilot can name are now the Profiles identities whose face recognition is switched on, matched ONLY against the reference photos authorized in each profile (sealed with `IDENTITY_ENC_KEY`, or kept in memory only). Pictures in the Images library — a person's folder, an album's reference pictures, photos already filed under them — no longer feed recognition or the description that steers it. A match at or above the file-by threshold is filed by; one between the thresholds shows Is this Brandy? Yes / No on the review card (and a flag on the Deck) and is not used until answered; below, the face stays unidentified. Filed photos carry `identityIds`, so the picture is tied to the person's profile without becoming part of it. The Photos tab's People list shows Profiles people as *From Profiles* (edit there); adding someone goes to Profiles. Every chat, the agent and the Autopilot chat get the same PEOPLE block (`src/lib/identity`), and each person is an `identity` memory for search, the MCP and the harness.

Bills, on the calendar (Nov 2026) — the Calendar has a Bills tab beside Month, holding every bill Jarvis knows about. Most are not typed here at all: they are read live out of the Profiles app, so a payment filed under a profile — the girlfriend's car insurance, the DTF printer's payment under Northside Prints — is on this tab without a sync step, and editing the row in Profiles edits the bill. A row becomes a bill only when it has an amount AND a schedule, so receipts and past purchases stay out. Filter pills per profile (plus No profile), order by date, highest first or A–Z, and a Show filter for what is still owed or only what is late. A $ still to pay statement leads, the unpaid bills sit under it as confirm cards, and every bill is a ledger row. The big grey tick turns green only after a confirm card naming the bill, the amount and the day — and the mark is per occurrence, so November's rent says nothing about December's. Calendar days carry a small amount chip per state (green paid, rose late, grey still coming) in both views, and the day panel lists that day's bills. Bills of your own are typed with Add a bill; a profile bill whose due day was never written down says "day not set" and can be corrected here without touching Profiles, and one that was never a bill can be taken off the list while its row stays in the profile.

One voice for the whole hub (Nov 2026) — the always-listening voice no longer lives only in Chat: it is mounted once in the root layout (`src/components/voice/VoiceProvider.tsx`), keeps listening across pages, and lives INSIDE the chat it is talking to (Jarvis itself keeps its reactor for the same voice). "Jarvis, …" goes to the chat or harness thread in use — Jarvis chat, Profiles, an open harness thread, a running build (Client Review / Website Studio), App Builder, Website Studio drafts, the Dashboard agent — and the answer is read back (a harness's answer when its turn finishes, or the gate it stopped at). With no chat on the page it types into the box you were in, and with no box it opens Jarvis and runs it here. Owner pages only, never inside a frame, only the visible tab listens. Only pages that have a Jarvis chat or harness thread have a microphone at all (Nov 2026) — the floating orb that used to put one in the bottom-left corner of every other owner page is gone (owner: "there is a microphone in every app on my jarvis, you can remove this; this is only for apps with a jarvis chatbot harness"), and with no chat on the page nothing listens even with Hands-free left on.

Start / stop, not always listening — nothing listens until you tap a chat's voice face (or Jarvis's mic): it hears ONE request, answers, and switches the microphone off by itself; Stop cuts listening and speaking at once. Always listening for "Jarvis" is Hands-free, an opt-in switch remembered on this device (Jarvis's "Wait for the name" is the same switch), so it never picks up a conversation in the room and starts a task.

A living 3D avatar, and one voice button (Nov 2026) — picked from three mockups (3, "Bold"). On an empty chat a big Three.js avatar floats over the box with ONE round voice button under it (the bar has no mic of its own until a conversation starts); once a conversation starts the avatar moves INTO the chat box as its one voice button (`components/voice/ChatVoiceAvatar.tsx`): tap the live face to talk, tap again to stop, and the small ▾ beside it opens a popover above it with the big avatar and the switches ("Transform every few seconds", "Always listen for Jarvis", "Speak answers aloud"), closed by a click elsewhere or Escape. Nothing floats over the page — the first version's top-right pill covered a navigation button (owner, 2026-11-22). On Jarvis tabs with no chat box the face sits in the bottom status bar. The old orb, the voice chamber, its Talk / "Wait for the name" / "Speak answers aloud" buttons and the hub's floating corner orb are gone. It is one procedural body that melts between nine forms (human, robot, wolf, cat, dragon, alien, orb, crystal, liquid blob) and six materials (hologram, glass, metal, plasma, solid, wireframe), with an energy surge at each change; on its own it transforms every 5 s, and a tap makes it flinch and change at once. It breathes, blinks and floats; its eyes follow the pointer anywhere on the page; it leans in while listening, its motes spin while it thinks, and its mouth is driven by the real Phonon audio (viseme from the analyser, word timing from the browser voice) with the answer's tone as a passing emotion; talked over, it flinches and shuts its mouth at once. Say or type "turn yourself into a blue holographic wolf", "change your eyes to glowing red", "make yourself smaller and float", "look happier", "keep transforming", "go back to normal" — the fast reader (`lib/new-jarvis/avatar/commands.ts`) does it with no model and no PC, and anything else goes to the agent's `avatar` tool. A chosen look is kept per account (`jarvis-avatar:v1`); emotions pass. A GLB/GLTF link can be worn instead of the body (loaded only then; viseme/blink morph targets and an idle/talk clip are driven if the file has them). It appears wherever a Jarvis chat harness is on the page — a registered voice target: Jarvis chat, Profiles, a harness thread, Website Studio drafts, App Builder, a running Client Review build, the Dashboard agent — and nowhere else — each of those chat boxes carries the face in place of its own mic (Profiles' Dictate mic and its bar's decorative orb are now the avatar); a page with no Jarvis chat has no voice button and no microphone. All avatars on a page run on one shared clock, so they always show the same form. Code: `src/components/new-jarvis/avatar/` (`AvatarScene.tsx` renderer, `shaders.ts`, `JarvisAvatar.tsx` hero + big voice button), `src/components/voice/ChatVoiceAvatar.tsx`, logic + tests `src/lib/new-jarvis/avatar/`. Off-screen or hidden it stops drawing; reduced motion stops the transforming; no WebGL shows a glowing core.

Two agents: 3D or Real (Nov 24 2026) — picked from three mockups (1, "Switch under face"). A small 3D | Real switch sits under the big avatar, and the same switch is in the popover of every chat box's face. Real is the real-looking agent: the AI Live Studio host's portrait (`RealFace.tsx`), breathing and swaying, a warm key light driven by Jarvis's own voice while he speaks and a cyan ring following yours while he listens — it reads the same analyser the 3D head reads. It moves no lips (a still can't; lip sync is LiveTalking's, on the PC, in AI Live Studio). The choice is the synced `face` setting in `jarvis-avatar:v1`, so the big avatar, every chat box and every device show the same agent. Say or type "switch to your real face" / "go back to 3D" (the fast reader, no model), or the agent's `avatar` tool sets `face`. Asking for a 3D look ("be a blue wolf") switches back to 3D so it shows; "go back to normal" keeps the chosen agent. If the 3D scene's code fails to load, the glowing core shows instead of the page crashing (`SceneBoundary` in `JarvisAvatar.tsx`).

The real face talks with real lip sync (Nov 24 2026) — when LiveTalking runs on this PC (`C:\dev\livetalking`, :8010, started with `--avatar_id alex_live --customvideo_config data/alex_moves.json`, see `tools/alex-moves`), the real face is Alex's live LiveTalking video and every spoken answer is said by him, lips moving: `useWakeVoice`'s `speak()` hands the WAV to a voice sink (`lib/new-jarvis/voiceSink.ts`) instead of playing it, and `lib/new-jarvis/avatar/liveFace.ts` sends it to `/humanaudio`, so the voice is heard once, from his stream. If the voice server (Phonon) is down, LiveTalking says the text in its own voice (`/human`, Edge `en-US-AndrewNeural`) — still lip-synced — before the browser's voice. ONE LiveTalking session per page (every face shares the stream; one audible copy), closed on page exit. Turn-taking waits for him to finish by the clip's own length (`avatar/wav.ts`) and `is_speaking`, so the mic isn't handed back mid-sentence. Per-device switch in the face popover, "Lip sync (LiveTalking on this PC)" with its live status; on by default everywhere the real face is picked (picking "Real" is the opt-in — the live site's face sat silent while it was localhost-only, Nov 24 2026). A "Lip sync" badge shows on the face while live, and a line under the 3D | Real switch always says why it isn't: "Lip sync is off · Turn on", "LiveTalking isn't answering on this PC · Try again", or "Lips and hearing on this PC — tap the mic and talk". The popover's face is a 4:5 portrait (240×300), never a wide strip: the wide box cropped Alex to forehead-to-nose with his mouth under the edge, so nobody could see him speak. While live, the video carries no breathing/sway/zoom, no bottom shade, and the badge sits top-left — his lips are the thing to watch. Measured: while his voice plays, the mouth region moves ~4× more than at rest (Wav2lip on a closed-mouth photo — real but modest). His voice starts about 3 s after the face says "Speaking" (LiveTalking's buffering). Same engine as the TikTok Live agent, so talking to it proves that pipeline.

The real face hears you on this PC too (Nov 24 2026) — while the lip-synced face is live and LiveTalking's own recognizer is on (SenseVoiceSmall at `ws://127.0.0.1:8010/api/asr`, needs `funasr` + `modelscope` in LiveTalking's venv), Jarvis listens through it instead of the browser's speech recognition, so your voice never leaves the machine (`lib/ai-live-studio/localRecognition.ts`: an energy voice detector with a learned noise floor and a 350 ms pre-roll, 16 kHz PCM per utterance). While you speak it sends a "…" interim mark so Jarvis doesn't end your turn early; the mark is never treated as words. The face popover says "he hears you and his lips move … all on this PC" when it's on. Recognizer off → the browser's, as before. Measured: "Make yourself look happier." transcribed exactly, ~0.4 s once warm.

The real face moves like a live streamer (Nov 25 2026) — Alex used to be one still photo, so he stared. Now he's a chest-up streamer at a desk with a coffee mug, and every frame is real video rendered free on this PC (`tools/alex-moves`: Flux 2 Klein base picture, then MiniMax H3 FL2VA clips that start and end on it). While quiet he blinks, glances at a second screen and smiles (LiveTalking's quiet loop). While talking his head nods and sways under the lip sync (avatar `alex_live`). Between lines he does short actions: sip, laugh, think, wave, lean in (`/set_audiotype`, `LiveTalking.act`). `lib/new-jarvis/avatar/moves.ts` picks them: after a line it reacts to the mood (a laugh after something funny, a wave on hello, the thinking pose on a question, ~70% of the time), and every 18–40 s of quiet he does something on his own (sip, think, lean, never the same twice running). `liveFace.ts` cuts an action short when he has to speak, because LiveTalking would otherwise finish it first. No action plays while he talks (a hand over the mouth breaks the lip sync).

Answers speak in the voice you picked — the hub voice sent `/api/tts` the text alone, so every spoken answer was Phonon's default voice; it now sends `ttsBody` with the Voice stage's voice, speed, expression and consistency, like the preview does.

Choose how Jarvis sounds — a Voice stage at the top of the Dashboard, above the memory core. All 37 English Phonon voices as cards with the catalog's own description, filtered by the accent the catalog actually states (British 8, American 3, Not stated 26) plus Characters (12). Press Hear <name> to audition one without keeping it, or pick the card to keep it; Speed, Expression and Consistency sit under the grid. The choice is saved per account (`voice-settings:v1`) and the status dock shows which voice is live. A preview goes through the same `/api/tts` and the same body (`ttsBody`) a real answer uses, so what you audition is what you get. With no voice backend running it says so in plain words and names the command to start one — it never fails silently.

Shell, memory core sphere, dashboard, memory tab — New Dashboard becomes Jarvis at /apps/jarvis; the old route redirects and the Four-Cs profile keeps its own store key, so no saved data moves. The memory core draws one glowing dot per real memory, c…

Moved into the hub as /apps/buildflip-2 — Brought over from legacymiles/buildflip-2-2 and the live v1: its route, UI, logic and API land in the hub's own folders, its AI goes through the shared provider, and its fonts come from the faces alr…
Built only after your PC has checked it, with the failing checks on screen
Profiles, accounts and the memory map
Show the file a write is touching
Keep a build brief to one line while it runs
The live line shows the newest thing, once
One live line while the coding harness works

Keep going when the tab closes, the bridge restarts, or a limit hits — A build was a harness thread in the bridge and a row on the server, but nothing on the PC remembered it. Closing the tab left the thread running invisibly; a bridge restart (an update, a wake, a rein…

Pick which Claude powers In Queue and 24/7 agents, and give the harness your keys once — One "Powered by" menu on every harness surface (24/7 agents, In Queue's Run now, the harness start panel; Chat lists the same picks): Claude Opus 5.5 / Opus 5 / Sonnet on your subscription, the same …
Carry on the moment this PC has power — The hub stores a goal and never pushes. This is the other half -- the thing on the PC that notices it has power and asks "is there anything I can do?".

24/7 agents that carry on where the last machine left off — Work that needs a MACHINE -- Flux on Pinokio, a Blender render, an Unreal build -- could only be asked for while the PC was awake. From a phone, or with Pinokio unreachable, it was a dead end.

A workbench in the chat — coding agents, GitHub, Vercel, Supabase, MCP, CLIs — The chat could browse, read and run, but it could not hand a multi-file job to an agent that writes, tests and commits, and it had no way to reach the services an app actually ships through. Both are…
Stop gating the push, stop refusing in silence, remember the act — Three failures from one real build, in order of what they cost.

Refresh arena scores daily, and show what a filter hides — A leaderboard whose scores are only ever typed in by hand goes quietly wrong, so the daily check now has two halves: Hugging Face for new releases, which still land in the inbox for approval, and Art…
mustKeep: Folder cards' hover Edit / Move / Delete, the Photos card opening Photos, Unfiled appearing only when something is loose, and the drawer tree on phones.
Auto-backup to Drive keeps running from the toolbar chip (the card component stays mounted).
Nothing is saved or moved into Folders by any chat without the owner seeing the content and the exact destination first and pressing Save / Apply (Full access excepted in the main chat).
Folders answers cite their sources with the full folder path; nested folders are never flattened.
The PC brain (`tools/jarvis-bridge/brain.mjs`) runs Claude Code with its built-in tools removed (`tools: []`) — leaving them visible is what produced "Reached maximum number of turns (1)".
Drive storage numbers come only from the account's own Drive API; never estimated.

Recognition only from Profiles. `buildContactSheet` is fed by `recognitionCast()` (`src/lib/identity/sync.ts`): enrolled identities with profile faces; Photos-tab refs of a linked person stay empty and `addPersonRef` refuses them; person-folder album refs are dropped. An unsure match never routes a photo (`gateFaces`, `src/lib/recall/photos/faceGate.test.ts`).

Jarvis still speaks. `useWakeVoice.speak` (and the older `useVoice.speak`) posts to `/api/tts` and plays the audio through an AudioContext, so the Reactor meter reads the voice and not the microphone. A media element that is routed into a context but never connected to `ctx.destination` goes silent.

The voice is always on, not a button. Wake word, talk-over mid-answer and the echo test are untouched by the Voice stage; the dock still says the voice *state* in words (off / waiting for its name / listening / thinking / speaking), with the chosen voice's name after it.

One voice button on screen. The empty chat has the big round button under the box and no mic in the bar; mid-conversation the avatar face in the bar is the only voice control. Every Jarvis chat (Profiles, App Builder, Website Studio, Client Review, a harness thread, the Dashboard agent) has the face and no second mic. Never two things that both start listening.

Nothing voice-related floats over a page. The avatar lives inside the chat box (or Jarvis's status bar); its popover opens only when asked and closes on a click elsewhere or Escape, so it can never sit on top of a navigation button.
The avatar never blocks the chat. It is lazy-loaded, stops drawing off screen and in a hidden tab, and a page with no WebGL gets a glowing core, not a blank box or a crash.

"Become a better cook" is not an avatar command. The fast reader only takes a sentence that addresses the avatar ("yourself", "your eyes", "turn into a <form>"…); everything else goes to the chat unchanged (`avatar.test.ts` pins the cases).
A chosen look survives a reload and another device, and "go back to normal" returns to the transforming default.

The lip-synced real face answers out loud — with LiveTalking and Phonon running here, a spoken request is answered by Alex's moving lips, heard once (never twice, never the browser voice), and Jarvis listens again only after he finishes. LiveTalking not running → the portrait, and Jarvis speaks as before. Phonon down → LiveTalking's own voice, still lip-synced.

A tapped mic keeps listening until you've spoken (Nov 24 2026) — tapping the mic waits up to 10 s for your first word (`FIRST_WORD_WAIT_MS` in `wake.ts`); the 1.1 s end-of-sentence pause only counts once something was heard. Before, the mic switched itself off 1.1 s after a tap — opening the mic through LiveTalking's recognizer alone takes about that long.

The galaxy gives the GPU to the real face (Nov 24 2026) — while the lip-synced face is live, the galaxy background (`WorldField.tsx`) drops to its light tier and draws at 24 fps. Measured on the owner's RTX 3050 laptop: the full galaxy took 99% of the GPU, which starved LiveTalking (its speech recognition took 88 s for 1.3 s of audio and its server stopped answering); yielding, the page takes ~28% and hearing is back to ~1 s.

Only the tab in front holds a LiveTalking face (Nov 24 2026) — LiveTalking allows 5 sessions and every open Jarvis tab held one, so the tab you were using was refused. A tab gives its slot back 15 s after it's hidden and takes one again when shown (`liveFace.ts`); a full LiveTalking shows "LiveTalking is busy — other open Jarvis tabs hold every face" instead of "isn't answering".
You can see his whole face talk — the popover shows Alex from forehead to chin, mouth in plain view, nothing (badge, shade) over his lips, on a laptop and at 390 px.

The real face works on the live site too — on the hosted Jarvis on this PC, picking Real connects to LiveTalking with no setting to find; a silent face always shows the reason and its one-tap fix under the 3D | Real switch.
Tapping the mic keeps it listening — after a tap the mic stays on through a pause of several seconds before you speak; it never switches itself off before you've said anything.
The real face talks while the galaxy shows — with the lip-synced face live, the background never starves LiveTalking: spoken requests are heard in about a second and answered on his lips.

Alex never just stares — with LiveTalking started on `alex_live` + `data/alex_moves.json`, he blinks and looks around while quiet, does a move on his own within about 40 s of quiet, and an answer never waits for a sip or laugh to finish. LiveTalking started without the moves → the set_audiotype calls do nothing and he talks as before.

Local hearing never cuts you off — with LiveTalking's recognizer on, a spoken request is heard whole (the turn stays open while you talk) and answered; recognizer down → the browser's speech recognition takes over with no error.

3D | Real switches everywhere at once — the big avatar, every chat box's face and its popover show the same agent, kept across reloads and devices; switching back to 3D never crashes the page, even when the 3D scene's code fails to load. "Switch the lights to real time mode" is not a face switch.
Spoken answers use the picked Phonon voice. `useWakeVoice.speak` sends `ttsBody(…, loadVoiceSettings())`, never the text alone.
No backend is not a crash. With nothing configured, `/api/tts` answers `{ fallback: true }` and the browser's own voice speaks; the Voice stage says what to start, in plain words.
A saved voice that no longer exists falls back. `clampSettings` drops a name the catalog does not have rather than sending it on every line.

A bill is never marked paid by one tap. The tick opens a confirm card naming the bill, the amount and the day; only the answer writes the mark, and it is keyed to that occurrence (`billId|YYYY-MM-DD`) — never to the bill as a whole.

Profiles stays the source for the bills it owns. `src/lib/bills/fromProfiles.ts` derives them on every read and never copies them into `jarvis-bills:v1`; the blob holds only typed bills, paid marks and the owner's corrections. A bill taken off the tab leaves the profile row alone.

A row needs an amount and a schedule to be a bill. "Gildan 5000 × 144 · $431.28 · Oct 30" is a purchase and must stay off the tab; "Shopify plan · $39.00 · Monthly" is a bill. Guessing the other way fills the calendar with things that are not bills.

The month grid still shows events. The grid moved into a shared `MonthGrid`, used by both views; events, clashes, the today pill and the selected day behave exactly as before, with the bill chips added under the date.

title: Tap Safe
whatItDoes: A tracker for the STD lab reports you already receive, and a way to show someone what you were tested for, what came back, and how long ago the sample was taken. Upload the PDF from STDcheck, Quest, Labcorp or MyChart and it is read server-side — lab, panel, collection date and each of ten results — then handed to you on a review screen where nothing is saved until you confirm every line. A phone photo goes to a vision model instead, and when there is no key it says so and drops to manual entry rather than pretending. The word "clean" appears nowhere in it. Status is derived per infection rather than per record, because someone may have had HIV drawn two weeks ago and syphilis six months ago, and one overall date would hide that; every row carries its own age, fresh under 30 days and stale past 90, and the ones nobody tested for stay on screen in grey so a two-test panel can never look like a full workup. Positives are first-class and carry treatment context — treated and cleared, undetectable, on suppressive therapy — because an undetectable viral load is not transmissible and flattening that into a red dot is both wrong and cruel. Sharing is a live handshake: you read out a six-character code, they type it, you see a preview of exactly what approving would show, and a yes opens it for 24 hours. Denials are silent, since a refusal that announces itself is a disclosure of its own, and rotating your code cuts everyone off at once. The report files are never shared — they carry a legal name and a date of birth — and no result page is without the two things it cannot prove: that the document is authentic, and that anything has happened since the sample was taken.

title: Jarvis Audio Studio
whatItDoes: Three music studios behind one switcher, because they were always three halves of the same job: get the recording, understand it, make the next one. FIND searches a song, names the exact recording first — album, year, length and thirty seconds of the real audio — and only then hunts a file for it, scoring every candidate against what you confirmed rather than the words you typed, so you stop ending up with a cover, a sped-up edit or a lyric video with a nine-second intro. Files come from the Internet Archive, the Creative Commons catalogues Openverse indexes, and roughly twenty sites through yt-dlp, grouped by what the licence actually lets you do with them. CLASSIFY is the private catalogue: paste a name or a link and it measures tempo and key off the preview in your own browser, files the song on a 1–10 energy ladder into a genre and a sub-genre, and describes it in whichever voice you asked for — plain English, producer, music theory, DJ, dancer — including a style prompt of that exact recording an AI song generator can follow. Upload your own audio and a listening model hears it rather than guessing from the filename. CREATE is the production side: write the brief, watch it become a style line and a lyric sheet, and render a real 48 kHz song on YuE2 — which plans before it plays, so the melody and chords come back as a score you can edit and re-render instead of rerolling the dice. A voice you save once is cloned, isolated from the music it arrived in, and kept in a library that never has to process that artist again. Switching studio never leaves the app or drops what you were holding, and every one of them works with no keys set: the catalogue, the measuring, the writing and the score editing all run locally, and only rendering asks for a GPU — which it says plainly when it is not there.

title: H3 Prompt Lab
whatItDoes:
The self-improving MiniMax H3 prompting lab (grown from H3 Experiments on 2026-11-24 — same slug, so old links work). There is ONE Master Prompt Guide and it publishes as ONE skill, `h3-prompt`. Experiments are not rival guides: each one changes a few of the compiler's techniques (knob = value: lead block, camera wording, identity handling, length, shot structure, set description, action writing, dialogue format, closing clause) on top of the guide's settings for a genre. Every test is paired — the same scenario rendered by the master and by the experiment with the same seed on the owner's own H3 in WanGP — and every clip is measured by ffmpeg on the PC (cuts, frame-to-frame SSIM, freezes, exposure, camera motion) before a vision judge scores what it sees with frame-numbered evidence. Credit goes to individual techniques (additive back-fitting, so techniques that travelled together split it), ranked by the lower bound of a 90% interval with shrinkage, so one lucky render cannot win. Techniques that clear the bar are combined per genre into a proposed guide change with its evidence; nothing changes the guide without approval (unless promotion is set to automatic), every version is kept, and rollback makes a new version.

Design spec: `docs/superpowers/specs/2026-11-24-h3-prompt-lab-design.md`. PC worker: `tools/h3-lab-worker/` (README there).
features: Run in 24/7 Queue (Nov 25 2026) — Video Reverse Engineering has a "Run in 24/7 Queue" panel (`research/QueueRunPanel.tsx`): upload a video (mp4/mov/webm/m4v/mkv) or paste a social link, say what to change (characters, outfits, locations, style) and how many variations, and it files an `h3-recreate` task. The VPS worker downloads it, finds shots with ffmpeg scene detection, extracts keyframes, runs this lab's own analysis (`server/brain.ts`) and recreate/compile/lint, and leaves a storyboard plus one H3 prompt per shot with variations in the task's Results — the page can be closed meanwhile. A link that cannot be imported asks for an upload instead.

Master Prompt Guide — v1 consolidates `h3-prompt` (everything in it survives), MiniMax's official base/Ref2VA formats, the measured long-video rules from the seesee75 Director paper (rules only; its GPL code is not used) and this PC's WanGP facts: 14 core sections + 43 genre modules across narrative, cinematic, action, gaming and commercial. Read it all, copy as SKILL.md, view any version, roll back.
Genre modules inside the one guide — each genre has its own compiler settings, scoring weights, rules, pacing, camera language and continuity list; the agent researches per genre.

Deterministic compiler + linter (`compile.ts`, `lint.ts`) — official base or six-section Ref2VA prompt from a shot spec and the bibles; the linter checks length per shot, two-positions, dialogue that cannot fit at 2.5 words/s, beats, duration, bracket camera tags, phantom references, missing sound, body contact and off-frame entrances.

Experiment Lab — experiments A–E seeded as drafts (character-first, environment-first, cinematography-first, structured scene-by-scene, hybrid) with hypotheses; the live compiler (the standout) rewrites the prompt instantly as technique switches are flipped and highlights what changed; queue paired renders, render once, save as an experiment.

Experiment Comparisons — technique leaderboard ranked by lower bound, per genre; side-by-side master vs experiment with videos, aligned judging frames, per-dimension deltas, prompt diff and owner ratings; the old skill-films ledger lives inside it.

Scoring — 11 dimensions, genre-weighted: measured (continuity by SSIM spikes against the clip's own baseline, so a steady fast push is not a morph; camera match; freezes; static-camera set stability; exposure) + judged (vision model, frame-cited) + owner overrides.

Continuity Inspector — measured and judged issues with severity, confidence, timestamp, evidence and a recommended prompt fix; changes the spec marks intentional (position, lighting, wardrobe, environment, props) are never flagged; across production scenes it compares the previous scene's end with this one's start.

Video Reverse Engineering — the browser finds the shots (colour-histogram cuts) and grabs keyframes; a vision model writes a blueprint (people, positions, actions, dialogue, emotion, camera, light, set, props, transitions); recreate it as a production with your own cast and sets — never a face swap. Without an AI key it stores the measured structure only and says so.

Character / Environment / Production bibles — explicit identity and layout fields, continuity rules, reference photos (sent to H3 as Ref2VA references, identity first); productions compile prompts frozen with the guide version, render per scene, and show the continuity strip between scenes.

Autonomous agent — `agent.ts` decides the next step (evaluate → conclude → combine → queue → design → research); it runs from the PC worker's idle tick, the open page, and a GitHub Actions schedule (`h3-lab-tick.yml`, only once `H3LAB_TICK_TOKEN` is set on GitHub and Vercel). Start / pause / resume / stop, run one step, daily render and AI budgets (owner renders are never budget-blocked), max concurrent experiments, manual or automatic promotion, hub AI or Claude Code (via the worker) as the brain. Offline experiment design picks the weakest genre-weighted dimension and tests ONE untested technique at a time.

H3 Connection — the PC worker (`tools/h3-lab-worker`) polls the hub with its own token (the site never calls the laptop), renders through the existing WanGP MCP on :42004 (never starts a second wgp.py), measures, uploads to Storage bucket `h3-lab` via a signed PUT, and re-queues renders it lost on restart. Diagnostics page with pass/fail rows.

Repository Research — the five researched repos plus the evaluation tools, with licence, compatibility, recommendation and integration status; the agent adds GitHub finds for review; nothing is installed automatically.

Jarvis Skill Integration — Publish writes the approved guide to the `h3-prompt` skill through the hub's skill store (the same store as the jarvis-memory connector), with up to three top-scoring prompts as examples.
Activity feed — every entry is written by the step that did the work; nothing is synthesised.

title: Image Studio
whatItDoes:
A studio of specialist image agents, each an expert in one look. Nostalgia turns you into a photo from any decade — 70s Polaroid, 90s disposable, VHS still. Glamour shoots sultry, magazine-grade editorial portraits. Family Portrait arranges everyone you upload into the photo you'd frame. Cartoon → Real brings any cartoon or anime character to life as a real person. GTA Life drops you into your most unhinged moments: wrestling bears, yacht chaos, headlining a stadium. Everything lands in a gallery you can filter by agent, download, or refine into the next round.

**Inspire** (`/apps/image-studio/inspire`) lives inside Image Studio: a public AI image inspiration library and prompt-building studio. Anyone can browse; any signed-in account gets a private library. The agents above stay owner-only. whatItDoes:

to go deeper. Jarvis is the way information gets in and gets found: the owner tells it things in
plain words (or drops photos in), Jarvis works out where each piece belongs and proposes the
changes, and nothing is saved until the owner taps Save. The chat is answered by the owner's
**Jarvis harness** on their PC (Claude or DeepSeek, through the local bridge) when it is on, the
hub's cloud model when it is not, and an offline reader with neither.

Design rule from the owner: show the current level, click to go deeper, use Jarvis to find or
manage anything. Not a dashboard, not a CRM, not a file manager — no charts, stats, sidebars or
tab bars.

Its one voice button is Jarvis's living 3D avatar (Nov 2026): at the start of the chat bar, in place of the old decorative orb, and in the open chat where the Dictate mic was (the Dictate mic is gone — one voice button, owner's rule). Your existing profiles come in — every Dashboard profile is imported once (businesses into My Businesses, people where they belong, accounts and passwords as private rows); the Life record is synced into My Profile every time Profiles opens, updated in place, its Work history becoming job profiles inside My Jobs. The examples clear themselves the moment real data arrives.
Read my screen feeds Profiles — it stays in the main Jarvis chat bar; what it saves to the Life record shows up in My Profile straight away (it fires `jarvis:record-changed`).

The one identity system (Nov 2026) — every person profile IS a Jarvis identity: its profile id is the one id Camera Autopilot, the Images library (Dashboard Folders/Photos), Jarvis Memory and the LLM harness use for that person (`src/lib/identity/`, spec `docs/superpowers/specs/unified-identity.md`). Renames, nicknames, the profile picture and face references flow out to all of them; nothing else can mint a person.

Synced with Folders, Memory and Photos — one way — each real profile gets a folder under "Profiles" in the Dashboard (nested and moved/renamed with it) holding a searchable note of its details (private rows left out); photos uploaded to a profile are copied to Photos › <profile>. Folders and copied photos of a person carry their identity id. Nothing comes back by itself: pictures in the Images library are not shown in the profile and can never become a profile picture or a face reference. The gallery's From Images library button lists that person's library pictures so the owner can pick some in — the only road from the library in.

Profile picture and face references — in a person's lightbox: *Make profile picture* and *Use for face recognition*; gallery tiles show a star / face badge. Person › Settings › Face recognition: the consent switch (off = their face data is deleted everywhere), the profile picture, the reference strip and *Add reference photos* (uploads straight into the profile).

Face recognition for Camera Autopilot — Autopilot matches new photos ONLY against the reference photos authorized in profiles, for people whose consent is on. Profiles › Settings › Face recognition holds the master switch, the two thresholds (file-by and ask-me), whether face data is encrypted (`IDENTITY_ENC_KEY`), possible duplicate people, and *Delete face data*. Faces the Photos tab already had were carried into the matching profile once (consent marked "carried over"); a person with no profile got one.

Jarvis knows who you mean — every Jarvis chat, the New Jarvis agent and the Autopilot chat get a PEOPLE block built from the identities (names, nicknames, relationship, safe facts), people the message names first, and a word that fits two people is flagged so Jarvis asks. Each person is also one `identity` memory (`identity:<id>`) so search, the jarvis-memory MCP and the harness find "who is Brandy". Photos dropped into the Profiles chat are run through recognition; a sure match decides where they are filed, an unsure one is only mentioned.

New profiles start from what is already known — "create a profile for my 3D printing business" searches Jarvis Memory and the Dashboard's folders, notes and photos first, files what it finds into the new profile (cited), puts it in the right parent (a teacher inside the child's School, a business inside My Businesses, a job inside My Jobs) and asks questions for that kind of profile: equipment with purchase date, seller and price, vendors, websites and which email is used for which site for a business; school, doctor and sizes for a child; anniversary and favorites for a partner; codes, coworkers and payday for a job. After saving, the chat stays with the new profile so the answers are filed there.

It looks things up for you (Nov 2026) — a question about the owner's *records* ("what's my son's teacher's email") is answered from the profiles as before. A question about how something *works* ("how do I set up the RIP software", "why won't it print white", "what temperature for the shaker") is searched on the web first and answered from real pages, each one shown as a Web source card under the answer. Search is free and needs no key or account — DuckDuckGo server-side, with the top two results opened and read in full, since a snippet names a page but can't give a setting. The split is deliberate: facts about the owner's life still come only from the outline and are never invented, and a researched fact is an answer, not a row — it is never written into a profile unless the owner asks. With nothing found, the chat says it hasn't checked rather than guessing a menu path.

It says what it would need to know — when a how-to question lands on a machine whose profile is missing the facts that would change the answer (no software, no consumables, no computer), the chat answers as far as it honestly can, then asks for the one or two that matter most for *that* question, with a half-sentence on why each changes the answer, offered as chips. Jarvis, four sizes — orb while scrolling, a bar on every page (`/` to focus; focus offers questions for the page), a peek card for quick answers, and a full conversation sheet.

Answers with sources — the answer first, then source cards with the path (`MY BUSINESSES › NORTHSIDE PRINTS › BUSINESS EMAILS`); tapping one flies there level by level and flashes the row. Photo answers show a strip and Open gallery.

Telling Jarvis things — one message can become several changes (a new profile, rows in it, a date filed in two places). They show as one card — "3 changes waiting for your OK" — with Save all, Review each (untick any) and Cancel. Follow-up questions come with quick replies.

title: AI Live Studio
whatItDoes:
A real-time AI host for a TikTok LIVE stream, and the owner's control room for it. The host (Alex by default) reads the chat and answers people by name, out loud — gifts and follows first, @mentions next, plain questions aged up so a busy room never starves them, repeats dropped, and a line of its own when the room goes quiet. Nothing a viewer types is read aloud until it passes moderation. The owner can answer any comment now, skip it, mute its sender, or type a line for the host to say word for word.

Design spec and plan: `docs/superpowers/specs/tiktok-live-voice-agent.md`, `docs/superpowers/plans/2026-11-23-tiktok-live-voice-agent-phase-1.md`.
features: Stage — 9:16, the host's portrait (`public/ai-live-studio/alex.jpg`, 145 KB) breathing and gently swaying; or LiveTalking's lip-synced WebRTC stream when picked under Avatar and running on this PC (`C:\dev\livetalking`, :8010). States: off air, listening, thinking, speaking, AI paused.

The key light (`data-standout="voice-light"`) — the light around the stage is driven per frame by the host's real audio level (AnalyserNode on Phonon/Fish audio or the LiveTalking stream); a speech-shaped envelope for the browser voice, which reports no levels. Opacity/transform only.

Live chat — newest at the bottom with auto-scroll and a "N new" pill when scrolled up (deliberate exception to U6: the brief asked for a real livestream chat). Viewers, events (gift/follow/share) and the host's own lines are three different objects; the line being spoken is highlighted.

Director (`src/lib/ai-live-studio/director.ts`) — priority (operator > gift > follow > mention > share > question > chatter) with ageing (+1.5/s), per-minute cap from Response frequency, 5-minute repeat window, 2-minute staleness, idle filler from Audience interaction, interrupts on higher priority, `drainDiscarded` so every passed-over comment says why.
Thinking ahead — while one line is spoken the next reply is already being written (`peek` + prefetch). Measured: thinking time 37% → 0%, reply speed 4.5 s → 0.1 s.

Moderation (`moderation.ts`) — harassment (incl. spaced-out spellings), links, phone numbers, emails, spam, and the owner's own word list, before the queue; unsayable usernames become "friend". The model's reply is moderated too.

Owner's hand — Answer now (passes the per-minute cap, starts writing its reply at once), Skip, Mute viewer, "Make Alex say", "Comment as a viewer" (demo only), Pause AI (can be armed before going live), Mute voice, End live with a 3-second confirm window.

Brain — `POST /api/ai-live-studio/reply`, owner-only, input checked server-side, 40 calls/min cap, 8 s timeout, canned line with no AI key, model `LIVE_STUDIO_MODEL` or `anthropic/claude-haiku-4.5`. A busy queue asks for one-sentence replies. Replies parsed by `reply.ts`, which strips made-up tool-call markup the model sometimes emits.
Voice — `/api/tts` (Phonon, Fish as its net) per sentence, next sentence synthesized while one plays; falls back to the browser voice with a plain-English notice.

Personality — 5 presets; name, persona, humour, energy, expressiveness, style, voice, speed, response frequency, audience interaction, blocked words, TikTok account, LiveTalking avatar. Every field changes behaviour; synced across devices (`ai-live-studio:v1`).
Status strip — health, comments source, face, voice, frame rate (render or real WebRTC stream fps), reply speed, comments waiting. Status = icon + word, never colour alone.
Stage only — the frame full screen with operator chrome hidden, for window capture.

Director booth (left column; below 1180 px it slides in from the top bar's Director button, full screen on a phone) — the owner's private side, in a cool blue (#8ab4ff) that never appears on the stage. A mic orb whose ring follows your voice (tap = Director Mode on/off; listening modes Always / Hold to talk (hold the orb or the ` key) / Only after "Alex"), a giant TALKBACK OFF/ON switch, where each voice goes (Talkback device vs the stream's device, pickable under Change, with the reason whenever Talkback falls back to text), the private thread (you on the right, Alex privately on the left, ✓ acks inline, "Which Mike?" choices, "Not sure I heard that right — apply it?" for unsure recognition), Performance (emotion chips, eye contact, head movement, reactions, standing notes and avoided topics with ×, Reset), the command bar with 8 types (Direction, Say exactly, Reply to comment, Reply to person, Change subject, React, Skip, Prioritize) and End session (stops the mic and Talkback; the stream and the direction carry on). Acks also float in the room's left gutter, never on the stage.

Chat for a director — a numbered Up next queue (answering now, then the order with the reason: gift, mention, question · waited, "Prioritized by you · note"); comments show new · selected · queued · answered · prioritized; the selected comment gets Answer next / Reply again, Instruct…, Reply to @user, Skip, Mute and History (everything that viewer said and Alex's replies). Every chat action is logged in the private thread.

The face performs — expression chip on the stage ("Sarcastic · eyes 8 · head 5"); the frame leans, tilts, sways by head movement and drifts off the lens by eye contact (`.als-perf`, transform/translate only); speaking speed follows the emotion.

Director engine — the owner directs Alex like an actor. `command.ts` turns natural speech ("be a little more sarcastic", "Respond to Mike next. Tell him that's a ridiculous question.", "stop talking about politics and ask everyone where they're from", "wait five seconds") into structured directions instantly and offline; anything it can't place goes to `POST /api/ai-live-studio/direct`, which returns the same checked shape. Names resolve against the live chat ("Mik" → @mike23; two Mikes → "Which Mike?"; nobody yet → answered the moment they comment). `performance.ts` holds the acting state (emotion, eye contact, head movement, reactions, standing notes, topics to avoid) and writes it into the public brain as a private block — the reply route rejects any line that would mention being directed (`leaksDirection`). The Director's cue lines ("ask the room…") are written by the brain from a private intent that is never itself spoken. `routing.ts` keeps Talkback off the stream: it only speaks on a different physical output device (compared by groupId, so "default" aliases can't fool it), else it answers in text; Alex's own words heard by the mic are dropped as echo.
Demo audience — a scripted room that exercises every rule (the brief's own conversation, a gift, a link, harassment, a repeat, a mention), then an endless seeded pool.
mustKeep: Go live with the demo audience: the host answers within a few seconds, and keeps answering.
A gift is thanked before older plain comments; the first question of the stream is still answered once it has waited.
"kys", links and the owner's blocked words are never spoken and show as hidden with a reason.
A repeated question is marked "Not answered — already answered a question like it".
Answer now puts that comment next, even at the per-minute cap.
With no comments, the host speaks up after the Audience-interaction delay.
No AI key → canned lines; no Phonon → browser voice; LiveTalking off → portrait. Never a silent stream, never a crash.
No markup is ever read aloud or shown as the host's line.
A director's instruction is never spoken, shown in the public chat, or acknowledged on air; a reply that mentions being directed is replaced before it airs.
Talkback never plays on the stream's device: when the two outputs can't be told apart (before mic permission, unplugged, same speakers) or the voice is the browser's, Alex answers in text.
With Talkback off, nothing in the booth makes a sound. Turning Talkback off never stops Director Mode; End session never ends the stream.

A new direction never cuts Alex off mid-sentence — it reshapes his next reply (the one written ahead is cancelled and rewritten). "Don't answer that" during that answer lets the current sentence finish.
A plain question to Alex ("what do you think of the audience?") never changes the show.
Nothing touches the microphone or the audio devices until the owner taps the mic or opens Change; Jarvis's own hands-free voice never listens on this page.
The page never scrolls sideways at 390 px, and the hub's voice orb stays off this page (it would hear the host).
requested: TikTok relay (`tools/tiktok-live-agent/`, plan Tasks 7–8) — the studio's side is built and listens on `ws://127.0.0.1:8787`; the relay that reads TikTok and forwards comments is next.

A real video of Alex (WanGP) would add head motion; the still loop already lip-syncs.

The director mic listens through LiveTalking's own recognizer (SenseVoiceSmall, `ws://127.0.0.1:8010/api/asr`) whenever it answers — `src/lib/ai-live-studio/localRecognition.ts`, shared with Jarvis's real face — so the director's voice stays on this PC. Turning Director Mode on checks for it first; not running → the browser's recognition as before. One-time setup: `uv pip install --python .venv/Scripts/python.exe funasr modelscope` in `C:\dev\livetalking` (first start downloads the model, ~80 s; ~0.4 s per utterance after).
Expression stills — real smiles/surprise need expression variants of the portrait (Flux 2 Klein in WanGP, free); until then expressions are performed by moving the frame.
Owner's mic (phase 2) and guest audio with an echo gate (phase 3).

A Preview shows it worn, folded, hanging and laid flat, and each picture downloads. An AI designer reads reference pictures and edits the actual layers when you press Apply. title: Baby No Scroll
whatItDoes: A child lock for a screen you are about to put in a small pair of hands. Pick a YouTube video or playlist, or one of eleven games, set a password, press Hand it over, and that one thing fills the screen with everything else taken away: no scrolling, no bouncing, no pinch, no pull-to-refresh, no long-press menus, no keyboard, no back gesture, and over a video no YouTube controls, no channel link and no wall of other videos at the end. The way back out is the parent's password: a dull steel key in a corner that must be pressed and held for over a second (a baby slaps, a baby does not press and wait), then a number pad the app draws itself, so the phone's own keyboard never opens. Three wrong tries and the pad makes you wait, longer each time, and it closes itself if left alone. Parents who prefer no password can switch back to the padlock, which opens only by being dragged an angle across two edges of the screen: along a line of widely spaced dots to the next corner, then a right-angle turn and along a second line of dots to the corner opposite. The dots have to be followed within a fingertip and nothing lights up on the way — no line fills, nothing glows, so the screen never demonstrates the gesture to whoever is watching. Stray off the dots, or let go anywhere along the way, and the lock goes straight back to its corner. A baby's thumb travels one way and stops, so it gets nowhere; a parent who knows the shape does it in a second. The games are built for a hand that cannot aim and every touch is correct: a racing sky of glossy balloons whose pops climb a musical scale, with gold balloons that set off fireworks and rainbow ones that split into a flock; a Musical Playroom with a toy shelf of six instruments (piano, xylophone, drums, harp, bells, bongos), one big instrument on screen at a time, all tuned so no mashing sounds wrong; rainbow soap bubbles; fireworks that launch to wherever a finger lands; squishy jelly friends with faces that wobble and bounce; a fish tank to feed; a toy-town road of beeping vehicles; peekaboo animals hiding in a meadow; neon finger paint that sings as it moves; eggs to crack open; and Silly faces, a Snapchat-style magic mirror where the front camera puts puppy ears, a crown or a lion's mane on the face it sees (tracked with jeeliz FaceFilter), a swipe changes the lens and an open mouth sets off its trick — the picture never leaves the device, and with no camera a cartoon buddy wears the lenses instead. Everything is drawn on a canvas at 60fps and every sound is synthesised in the browser, so there is nothing to download and it works on a plane. It is honest about its ceiling: a web page cannot disable a home button, so the setup screen tells you to install it and put Guided Access or Screen Pinning underneath it for a device you actually walk away from.
features: Parent password — set on the console before the hand-over (4–8 numbers, typed twice, refuses `1111`/`1234`-style runs). Stored only as a salted SHA-256 hash, never the digits. Hand it over stays disabled until one is set.

Password gate on the locked screen — a steel key in the chosen corner: press and hold 1.2 s to open the in-app number pad (a tap only wiggles it; triple-tap moves it to the next corner). Checks the moment the last digit lands. 3 wrong tries → 30 s wait, doubling to a 5 min cap, kept for the life of the tab. Pad closes itself after 20 s untouched. A real keyboard's digits and Backspace work too.

Angled drag lock (optional) — the padlock dragged along two dotted lines on two edges of the screen with a right-angle turn between them, chosen under "How it unlocks". A tap shows the dots; they put themselves away after 4 s. Nothing on the locked screen responds to the drag: no lit line behind the puck, no travelling pulse, no glow on the lock, the corner or the far end (owner, Nov 2026: "it shouldnt glow and show the line while unlocking") — so the screen never shows a watching child how far a drag got, or that it was getting anywhere. The second leg only starts counting once 96% of the first has been travelled, the turn cannot be undone mid-drag, and a finger more than 48 px off the edge it is following throws the drag away and sends the lock home — so one diagonal swipe to the far corner, a cut corner, or a sloppy traverse opens nothing. Letting go sends it home with a knock, wherever the finger is when it happens: the release is heard on the window, not just on the lock, so a finger that slides off the edge of the screen cannot leave the lock parked halfway. "Hold at the end" adds a second on the last corner; off by default, since the path is the safeguard. Keyboard: focus the lock and hold Enter for 1.8 s.
YouTube — one video or playlist, no controls, no end-screen wall, loop forever, saved shows newest first.

Balloon pop — canvas sky of glossy balloons racing up past clouds; touch pops (shards, confetti, shockwave), tap empty sky inflates a new one from the finger, dragging pops everything it crosses, quick pops climb a pentatonic melody, gold balloons fire fireworks, rainbow balloons split into five.

Musical playroom — toy shelf of six instruments (piano, xylophone, drums, harp, bells, bongos); one fills the screen at a time; every pitched one is pentatonic; dragging plays every key/bar/string crossed; remembers the last instrument.
Bubbles · Fireworks · Jelly friends · Aquarium · Zoom zoom · Peekaboo — six more canvas games, every touch anywhere answered instantly with picture and sound.

Silly faces — the front camera as a magic mirror (jeeliz FaceFilter, npm `facefilter`, Apache-2.0; model served from `public/baby-no-scroll/face/`). Camera light goes off when the game closes; nothing is recorded or sent.

Hide and seek — six eggs to crack.

title: Search Infrastructure
whatItDoes:
The web search every other app in this hub calls, so none of them holds a provider or a key. A
request walks a chain: SearXNG on this machine first, SearXNG on the VPS next, DuckDuckGo, then
Tavily — so searches are free and private while the laptop is on, keep working from the VPS when
it isn't, and only reach a paid provider when nothing self-hosted is reachable. Three typed
questions come out of it — web, news and research — and every answer has the same five fields
whichever provider served it: title, URL, description, source, and a publication date when the
page gave one.

The part that makes it usable by an agent rather than a person is extraction: ask for it and the
top results come back with the pages actually read and reduced to text, which is the difference
between a list of links and something a model can answer from. Identical searches are cached,
every caller has a per-minute and per-day ceiling, and an endpoint that fails three times in a row
is skipped for a minute rather than being waited out on every request — which is what stops a
sleeping laptop adding eight seconds to everything.

The console shows the chain as a rail with the path a request actually took lit up, the
hour-by-hour traffic split into live and cached calls, which app is spending the quota, and the
plain-English reason any instance is down — including the one everybody hits, where SearXNG serves
HTML until `json` is added to its formats list. Agents, crons and other repos authenticate with a
service key issued here, shown once and stored only as a hash; nothing but the server ever holds a
provider credential.

Full API reference: [`docs/search-api.md`](../search-api.md). SearXNG install:
[`infra/searxng/README.md`](../../infra/searxng/README.md).
features: The provider chain, ordered by cost and control — laptop SearXNG (free, private, local-only), VPS SearXNG (free, always on), DuckDuckGo (free, keyless), Tavily (paid). A localhost endpoint fails fast from anywhere else, so the dev chain and the production chain differ without a branch in the code.

Circuit breaker, half-open on the last hop — three consecutive failures and an endpoint is skipped for a minute; the final provider in the chain is tried even with its breaker open, so a failure is never returned while something untried might have worked.
Three typed questions — `web`, `news` (news category, dates on most rows), `research` (20 results, several SearXNG pages, Tavily's advanced depth and a generated answer).

Standardized results — title, URL, description, source, `publishedAt`, and a `score` normalized to 0–1 across providers. SearXNG's native score is an unbounded sum of engine weights, so it is divided by the top score in the same response.

Page extraction — `extract: 3` reads the top three results and returns the readable body, word count, author, site name and published date. Dependency-free (prefer `<article>`/`<main>`, then score blocks by paragraph density), with Tavily's renderer as the fallback for pages that only work with JavaScript. A page that cannot be read comes back with a sentence, not an exception.

Caching with hit accounting — in-process plus Supabase, keyed on everything that changes the answer and nothing that doesn't, so two different apps asking the same question share one hit. Extracted text is cached too, since it is the expensive half.

Rate limits and usage tracking — per-caller minute and day ceilings, counted atomically in Postgres so parallel calls cannot slip past, and one usage row per call carrying the caller, the app, the provider, whether it was cached, the latency and any error.
Service keys — minted in the dashboard, shown once, stored as SHA-256. Own limits, own scopes, own usage row. A key can never mint another key.

The routing rail — the page's one standout: the chain drawn as stations with the path a request took lit in indigo, failed hops struck in red, open breakers dimmed with their cooldown, and a pulse that replays the last test search along the path it travelled.
Test bench — runs a real search against the same public endpoint an app uses, with the provider pinnable and the cache skippable, and shows the attempts that drive the rail.

Keys that belong to people — a key is issued to an email address with its own plan (`owner` / `member` / `trial`), its own per-minute and per-day ceiling, and an optional expiry. A member's ceiling is far below the owner's on purpose: small enough that one person cannot empty a paid provider's balance. A key issued to someone else can never land on the owner plan even if the request asks for it.

Issued before they have an account — the key attaches to their Supabase account the first time they sign in with the address it was issued to, and never moves between accounts after that, so a second sign-up on the same address cannot take one over.

A member's own page (`/apps/search-access`) — reachable without the owner gate, because the people it exists for are by definition not the owner. Shows what they hold, their ceiling, what they have used and how to call the API. Never a key, never a provider name, never a hint that anyone else exists.
The People panel — one row per person holding a key: plan, calls, failures, last seen. Usage rows carry the address, so it survives the key being revoked and replaced.

Demo mode that is honest — with no Supabase service-role key the service still searches and still caches; the dashboard says the cache and counters are per-instance and keys cannot be issued, rather than failing oddly.
mustKeep: Every app keeps searching when a provider dies. The chain plus the breaker is the whole point; a single provider's outage must never surface to an app as "no results".

`lib/web/fetchPublic.ts` keeps its two exported shapes (`searchWeb` → `SearchHit[]`, `readPage` → `PageRead`). Jarvis's web tools and Profiles research depend on them and must not have to know the engine underneath moved.
A provider credential never reaches a browser. Keys are read server-side only; the dashboard is a client of the public endpoints, never a privileged view.

The extract endpoint refuses private network addresses, on every hostname's every resolved address and again after redirects. It takes a URL from a caller and fetches it server-side, so this is the control that keeps it from being an SSRF.
A service key cannot mint a service key. `/api/search/keys` and `/api/search/cache` stay owner-session only, and stay out of middleware's token-auth list.
`searchWeb` in `fetchPublic` never throws. Both callers are AI tool loops where a thrown error fails a whole turn but an empty result lets the model try another way.

A key issued to someone else is never on the owner plan. `planForRecipient()` enforces it and has its own test; honouring an explicit `owner` on a key for another address would hand a stranger the whole paid-provider balance.
`/apps/search-access` stays an EXACT public path, never a prefix — a prefix opens everything beneath it. The owner's console at `/apps/search-infrastructure` stays owner-only.
`/api/search/account` returns only the caller's own keys and usage. Never the provider list (it would leak the VPS hostname), never anyone else's keys.
A hub account is not access. A signed-in non-owner is a caller only if the owner has issued them a key; otherwise they are told to ask for one.

A result is a page, or it is dropped. `serveableUrl` in `providers/base.ts` — on the path every adapter returns through — refuses a search engine's own click-through, an ad network's tracker, a non-http URL and anything over 400 characters. Found by BuildFlip: `duckduckgo.com/y.js?ad_domain=amazon.com…` arrived as the top result for a lumber price, titled "Amazon Official Site", on its way to becoming a buy link on a build plan. The root cause was upstream of every provider — `unwrapDdgLink` followed DuckDuckGo's `/l/?uddg=` redirect onto an ad without re-judging the target — so the parser is fixed too, which fixes Jarvis's web tools and Profiles research with it.
The SearXNG 403 keeps its own message. "Add json to the formats list" rather than "the VPS is down" — it is the mistake everybody makes once, and naming it is worth a branch.
requested: Members can't rotate their own key. Today only the owner issues and revokes; a member who loses a key has to ask. Self-serve rotation is the obvious next step.
No sign-up flow. Access is granted by the owner issuing a key to an address, not by anyone requesting one. There is no "request access" button and no email to them — you send the key.
No billing. Plans are ceilings, not prices; nothing charges anyone and nothing is wired to Stripe.
Embeddings / semantic recall over past searches. The usage table already holds every query; nothing reads it back as a corpus yet.
A per-app quota rather than a per-caller one. Today an app's ceiling is the ceiling of whichever key or session called it; the `app` label is tracked but not enforced against.

title: 24/7 Queue
whatItDoes:
The command center for every ongoing, scheduled and autonomous AI task in the hub — the upgrade
of In Queue. The owner tells Jarvis what they want in plain words; Jarvis works out which app it is
about, which agent should do it, whether it is a one-off, a scheduled job, a recurring task or a
standing 24/7 workflow, splits big requests into parts that wait for each other, and files real
tasks. A worker on the VPS runs them with the PC off and the browser closed, and the board shows
what is actually happening — every status, progress bar, log line and result comes from a worker
that did the work.
features: Persistent task engine — every task, run, log line, finding, message and notification is a Postgres row (`queue_*` tables). Tasks survive refreshes, closed browsers, server restarts and network drops.

VPS worker (`tools/queue-worker`, Docker, `restart: always`) — claims due tasks with `queue_claim` (FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED: no task ever runs twice), runs one bounded step at a time under a renewed lease, saves state between steps, retries with exponential backoff, recovers a crashed worker's task when its lease expires, hands tasks back on shutdown, heartbeats its load/memory/running tasks. Concurrency per worker and per executor, memory ceiling, capabilities (a task only goes to a worker that can run it). Any number of workers.

Kinds — once, scheduled (at a time), recurring (every N minutes / daily at HH:MM in a zone), continuous (a standing workflow that resumes from its own saved state every round and survives a bad round).
Sub-tasks and dependencies — a multi-part request becomes parts plus a parent that waits for them and writes one report.

Jarvis commander — `/api/queue247/command`: one AI call plans tasks or acts on existing ones (pause, resume, stop, reschedule, answer), refuses duplicates of running work, uses past results and findings as memory. With no AI available an offline planner takes the words literally and says so. Also the Jarvis chat tool `queue_command` and connector tools `task_list` / `task_get` / `task_command` for Claude Code.

The stage — Jarvis's chat as the front of the page (mockup 3 "Chat is the stage", picked 2026-11-25; taste-skill Cold Luxury: smoke + silver, one emerald accent, Geist). A WebGL trail reveal (`QueueStage.tsx`, webgl-trail-reveal): calm smoked glass over the circuitry the agents run on; the pointer paints a trail that scans it in, labels for the real workers and 24/7 workflows light up under the trail, and every new queue event pulses out of its node. Reduced motion / no WebGL: a still picture of both layers. On it, Jarvis's message box (`JarvisComposer.tsx`): reference pictures (attach, paste or drop, up to 6, shrunk in the browser, stored in `queue-247` under `refs/<uid>/`, shown to the planner and kept on every task the message files as `config.references`), the model router (Auto = the hub's router, one-tap Opus 5.5 / DeepSeek V4.1, or any OpenRouter model from the full list; cloud models only — the "my subscription" brains need the PC), "Start talking to Jarvis" (talk-to-type) and Send. The conversation under it shows your pictures, which model planned each reply, and a live card per task filed. Tasks are a timeline rail on the left, counts / last hour / workers / discoveries / live activity on the right (phone: chat, tasks, then the rest).
Talk about a task — each task has its own conversation; words to a waiting task answer it, words to a busy one become guidance its executor reads next step.
Owner controls — pause, resume, edit, prioritise, run now, restart, terminate (cascades to sub-tasks), approve / decline, answer, delete.

Agents (executors): research (web/news/GitHub, never reports the same source twice), MT4 bot discovery (continuous; public Telegram channel previews, GitHub, web; static MQ4/MQ5 analysis for martingale, grid, averaging, hedging, repainting, missing stops, DLL imports, web requests, account locks, time bombs, obfuscation; quality/reliability/risk/strategy scores with reasons; fingerprint de-duplication and version lineage; notifies on notable bots; never runs EA code, never trades), H3 recreation (upload or social link → ffmpeg shots and keyframes → H3 Lab's analysis → storyboard → per-shot H3 prompts with the owner's changes + variations), monitor (alerts only on change), code change (files a 24/7 agent for the PC harness and mirrors it), connected app (outside apps do the work and report back), rollup.

Connected apps — every hub app is recognised from the catalog automatically; outside websites register in Apps, get a `q247_` key (hash stored) and use `/api/queue247/v1/*` (`docs/queue-247-api.md`): submit tasks, receive work at a callback, report progress, logs, findings, completion, questions.
Research library — every finding searchable by kind, app, text and score.
Notifications — notable discoveries, questions, approvals and failures.
mustKeep: A task filed on the board or from Jarvis chat appears at once and is claimed by the VPS worker within seconds when one is online; with no worker online the board says so instead of showing fake progress.
Pausing or terminating a running task stops it within a minute (lease renew fails → step aborted).
A worker restart never loses or duplicates a task.
The MT4 agent never executes downloaded code and never connects to a trading account.
Outside apps only ever see their own tasks.
In Queue requests and 24/7 machine agents keep working in their own tabs.
A message with pictures files its tasks with every picture in `config.references`, even when the AI planner is unavailable (the reply says nothing looked at them).
The model picked in the chat is the model that plans (the reply names it); "/" focuses the box.
